text:
Excited to share that I've been promoted to Senior Software Engineer.

Three years at this fintech startup went by fast. I joined knowing just enough to be useful, and most of what I've learned since then is how payments actually fail, how to ship without creating a mess for the next person, and how much of this job is just saying the thing clearly.

Grateful to the people who handed me harder problems before I felt ready for them, and to the teammates who made the rough weeks easier. Looking forward to what's next.

Some news: I'm leaving Deloitte to start my own consulting firm.

It's exciting, and a bit terrifying, which feels like the right mix. I don't have a polished origin story. I got to a point where I knew the kind of work I wanted to do and the way I wanted to do it, and the honest next step was to go do it under my own name.

Deloitte gave me clients I wouldn't have reached, problems bigger than I was, and colleagues who made the long weeks bearable. I'll miss the people. I will not miss every status meeting.

If you're building something and want another pair of eyes on strategy or the messy middle of getting it done, send me a note. And if we worked together: thank you. You made this feel possible.

Last month I was laid off. I sat on it for a few weeks before posting, mostly because I didn't know what I actually thought yet.

A few things that turned out to be true:

The job wasn't my whole identity, but it was my routine, a lot of my social life, and my sense that the week was going somewhere. Losing all of that at once is disorienting even when you know, on paper, that you'll be okay.

People show up in uneven ways. A few folks I barely knew sent introductions. A few people I expected to hear from didn't. I'm trying not to build a theory out of either one.

And the story I told myself in the first two days was worse than the facts. The facts are simple. I did good work, the company made a business decision, and I get to decide what I do next.

If this happened to you recently, you're not behind. You're just in the part people don't post about until it's already over.

Most companies get remote work wrong because they kept the office and deleted the building.

Same hours. Same meetings that should have been a paragraph. Same habit of promoting whoever is easiest to notice, which now means whoever talks the most in Slack.

The teams I've seen handle it well are almost boring about it. They write decisions down. They're specific about what actually needs to be live. They look at the work, and they don't treat a green dot like a personality.

Remote isn't a perk you add to an office culture. If you don't change how decisions get made and how people get judged, you just end up with a lonelier office that happens to be in everyone's kitchen.

We're hiring two backend engineers in Berlin.

The stack is Go and Postgres. The work is the kind where correctness matters and "we'll clean it up later" tends to become the outage. We're a small team, so you'd own real parts of the product, not a queue of tickets someone else specified to death.

If you like finding out why a query got slow, talking through tradeoffs in plain language, and leaving code other people can change, I'd like to hear from you.

Comment or message me and I'll send the details. Also happy to pass along good people if the timing isn't right for you.

My first manager taught me something I still think about.

I assumed a good manager had the answer and handed it to you. She rarely started there. She'd ask what I thought, wait long enough that I had to actually come up with something, and then point at the weak part without making it about whether I was smart.

What I got out of that wasn't a set of tips. It was practice at deciding. When I got it wrong, we talked about the decision. She didn't turn it into a verdict on me.

I didn't love it at the time. I wanted her to just tell me what to do. Now when I'm the one people are waiting on, I notice the urge to hand over the answer, and I try to pause.

Still working on the pausing.

We closed a $4M seed round led by Accel.

I'm happy, and mostly I'm grateful. Grateful to the customers who used the product while it was still rough around the edges. Grateful to the team that kept shipping while the fundraise took over the calendar. And grateful to Accel for backing us this early.

The round doesn't make the company. It gives us time to build what we said we were building, and to hire a few more people who care about it.

If you've been following along, thank you. We're hiring, and we're still early.

AI is changing marketing, just not in the way the keynote version suggests.

The tools got very good at making more. More posts, more variants, more emails that sound like someone who has read a lot of marketing emails. That's useful. It's also why a lot of brands are starting to sound like the same brand.

What actually moved, for me, is the cost of trying something. You can test a message in an afternoon that used to take a week of drafts and approvals. So the scarce part isn't production anymore. It's whether the thing is worth saying, and whether you know who it's for.

I don't think the job goes away. I think people who were mainly good at producing volume are going to feel it, and people who actually know their customer are going to get faster.

Which is slightly annoying, because knowing the customer was always the hard part.

The new mobile app is live.

Really proud of this team. It took longer than we wanted, and it's better because people didn't skip the parts they were tempted to skip. Thank you. Go download it and tell us what's broken.

Five things I wish someone had told me earlier as a junior developer:

1. Read the code around your change before you add more. A lot of my early bugs were me rebuilding something the next file already did.

2. Ask sooner than feels comfortable. People are less annoyed by the question than by finding out on day three that you went the wrong direction.

3. Write down what you changed and why. Your reviewer, and you in three months, will care about that more than about a clever line.

4. Getting stuck is normal. Staying stuck quietly is the part that hurts you.

5. You don't have to know everything. You do have to know how to look it up, and when a person will be faster than a search.

None of this is glamorous. Most of getting better isn't.

My first startup failed after two years.

We had a few customers who really liked it, a lot of meetings that felt like progress, and not enough revenue to support the story we were telling. We shut it down.

The honest part: I waited too long to admit it wasn't working. I confused being busy with getting somewhere. I hired before we knew what people were actually buying. And I liked the idea of being a founder more than I liked looking at the numbers.

I also learned that I can do hard things with people I trust, that a clear ending beats a slow one, and that plenty of advice you get in the middle comes from people who don't have to live with it.

I'm glad I tried it. I'm also glad I stopped. If you're in one of these and it isn't working, you're allowed to say that out loud.

Mental health at work is easy to put on a slide and awkward to deal with on a Wednesday.

I've had stretches where I looked fine in meetings and wasn't fine the rest of the day. The work still got done. Nothing obvious was on fire, so nothing got said. A lot of workplaces are set up to notice a missed deadline and miss the person.

What helped me wasn't a campaign. It was a manager who noticed and moved something without making me argue for it. It was being able to take a day without writing an essay. It was coworkers who didn't treat rest like a lack of commitment.

If you manage people, the useful version is pretty plain: notice, ask, and don't punish the honest answer. I'm not great at it. I'm better than I was, and I wish more teams treated that as part of the job instead of a perk.

Years ago I called a company about a billing mistake. It was about forty dollars. The person who answered fixed it in a couple of minutes, then stayed on the line until I understood why it had happened.

I still remember that company. I couldn't name three vendors I've spent much more money with.

What it taught me is that people don't remember your process. They remember whether their problem was treated as an interruption or as the work. The mistake cost them a little money and a little time. The way it was handled is why I stayed.

A lot of "customer experience" talk is more complicated than the thing itself: a person with enough context to help, and permission to fix it without sending you somewhere else. That version is harder to scale than a new tool, which is why so many companies buy the tool.

I just finished my MBA at INSEAD, and I keep thinking about the people around it more than the diploma.

My family put up with a year of me being half somewhere else even when I was home. Friends read things, talked me out of a few bad ideas, and reminded me to eat. Classmates turned the group work into the part I'll actually remember. A couple of professors pushed, which is different from just marking the paper.

Thank you. The degree has my name on it. The year worked because you were in it.

If I still owe you a coffee, I know. I'll get there.

Hustle culture's real product isn't hard work. It's the performance of never stopping.

Working hard is fine. I've done it when the work called for it, and I'll do it again. What's being sold is something else: that being exhausted proves you want it, that rest is a reward you cash in later, and that a quiet week means someone busier is passing you.

A lot of the loudest versions of this are about being seen working. The full calendar. The early-morning post. An identity built on being unavailable.

The take I'd actually defend is narrower. Busyness is a weak signal. Some of the best work I've watched came from people who guarded their attention, turned things down, and were willing to look less in demand on an ordinary Tuesday.

If a team only rewards the people who never log off, it isn't selecting for great work. It's selecting for who can absorb the damage.

The newsletter crossed 10,000 subscribers this week. I refreshed the number more than once.

It wasn't a clever funnel. I wrote every week for a long time while the list was small enough to feel silly, and a few readers kept sending it to one other person.

What actually mattered: writing to a specific person instead of "everyone in the industry." Subject lines that said what the thing was about. Deleting the intro I was proud of. Replying when people wrote back, including when that was twenty people.

What mattered less than I expected: the perfect signup page, announcing it constantly, and waiting until I felt ready.

If you're at a few hundred and it's quiet, it is quiet. That part doesn't go away by optimizing it. You just keep showing up.

Most networking advice is written for people who like networking. If you don't, you can ignore a lot of it.

You don't need to work a room. A few conversations you can actually tolerate will do more. What I tell friends who dread this:

Pick one person you want to talk to, not a target count. Leave when you're done. The next day, send a note about the specific thing you discussed. "Great to connect" is how both of you forget.

Smaller is easier. Dinner with six people beats a mixer with two hundred. Asking what someone is working on beats reciting your background. And a thoughtful message counts. It doesn't have to happen next to a lanyard.

People remember the person who listened and then said one useful thing. They forget the person who delivered a bio.

Working in sales taught me a few things I still use, and most of them aren't about selling.

Nobody owes you a reply. "Let me think about it" is often a no said politely, and pushing harder rarely changes that. The first reason someone gives you is often not the real one, so you learn to wait for it.

Rejection gets boring before it gets painless. Once it was boring, I stopped treating every no like a comment on me. That turned out to matter outside of quota too.

And being clear is a form of respect. Telling someone it isn't a fit saves both of you a month of vague follow-ups. I wish more situations worked like that.

I don't miss every piece of the job. I do miss how little room it left for pretending things were fine when they weren't.

We just hit 1,000 volunteers.

It's a strange number to stand next to. Big enough that I can't picture every person. Small enough that I remember when we were hoping ten people would show up on a Saturday.

This belongs to the people who came back. The ones who drove across town, showed a new volunteer what to do, and took the jobs that never make the photo. Our staff is small. The work happens because people decided it was worth an evening or a weekend.

If you've given time, thank you. If you've been meaning to, there's room. We have more to do than we have hands for, and that's a good problem only if people keep raising their hands.

I'm back at work after parental leave.

The first week felt like returning to a job I used to know how to do. The inbox had a lot of opinions. My attention was somewhere else a lot of the time. I sat in the car for a few minutes one afternoon and didn't go in right away.

What helped: people who caught me up without turning it into a quiz. A ramp that was actually slower, not just called a ramp. Room to be reachable for the baby and still be taken seriously in the room.

What didn't help: being told I must be so rested. I wasn't.

I'm glad to see the team. I also miss the other part of the day. Both of those fit in the same week. If you're about to come back, the weirdness is normal. It gets more familiar. It doesn't snap back on Monday.

Can anyone recommend a CRM for a small agency?

We're about eight people. I need something that keeps track of leads and clients without becoming its own project. A pipeline, simple reporting, and email that feels like part of the product. I don't need an enterprise suite, and I'd rather not spend a quarter setting one up.

If your team uses something you don't groan at, tell me what it is. Even better if you can say what started to annoy you after a few months. That's usually the review I can't get from the website.

I'll share back what I hear in case other people are shopping too. Thank you.

Product managers should learn enough SQL to answer ordinary questions without waiting on someone else.

Not "become the analyst." Just enough to open the data and check how many people did a thing last week, while you still remember why you asked.

It isn't only about speed, though the speed is nice. Your questions change once you can see how the data is shaped. You stop requesting a chart that hides the actual question. You notice when a number smells wrong before it ends up in a review.

It also makes the conversation with engineering and data more concrete. You can talk about the table and the weird edge case instead of pointing at a metric and hoping.

The useful slice is learnable. The rest can stay with people who do this every day. You just don't want to be stuck every time you need a number.

Deep Work by Cal Newport changed how I think about a workday more than any other book I've read on the subject.

The line that stayed with me: focus without distraction is getting rarer, and rare things become valuable. That sounds obvious until you audit a normal day. Mine was a string of small replies. I was busy. I was rarely inside the task that needed a quiet hour.

I didn't follow every rule he lays out. I did start protecting a block of time the way I'd protect a meeting I couldn't move. The work from those blocks was clearly better than what I squeezed in between messages.

The uncomfortable bit was how many of the interruptions were mine. The book didn't fix my job. It made it harder to blame the calendar for the whole thing.

Worth reading if your days feel full and your best work only happens by accident.

I've been a nurse for ten years today.

I don't have a clean lesson from it. I have shifts. Some I still replay on the drive home. A lot of them were just an ordinary hard day, which is its own skill: show up, be decent to people who are having a worse one, and do it again tomorrow.

Patients remember if you listened. Families remember if you told them the truth in a way they could hold. The people on shift with you remember if you came when they called. The chart is what the system counts. The rest is the work.

I've gotten faster. I pay attention to whether I'm getting numb, because that's the risk nobody puts in the anniversary post. The nurses who trained me, and the ones newer than me, are a big part of why I'm still here.

Ten years is a long time. I'm proud of the people who do this.

The biggest mistake I see in interviews isn't a wrong answer. It's treating the hour like a performance.

Candidates recite. They tell a smooth story about a project and never land on what they personally did, what broke, or what they'd change. When I ask a follow-up, they restart the script instead of answering the question I asked.

The people who stand out can slow down. They think out loud. They'll say they don't know and then tell me how they'd find out. Their questions sound like they've pictured the job, not like they saved three impressive ones for the end.

I'm not grading for polish. I want evidence we could work through a messy problem together. If the story could be dropped into any company, I still don't know why you want this one.

Bring the real example, including the part that was hard.

Next Thursday I'm running a free webinar on cloud cost optimization.

I'm going to skip the vague "finops journey" version. We'll look at where the bill actually grows: stuff nobody owns that's still running, storage everyone forgot, and the service that was temporary sometime last year. I'll show the checks worth doing first, and a couple that look smart and mostly waste an afternoon.

It's an hour. The aim is a short list you can use the following week.

The link is in the comments if you want a seat. Bring a charge you're irritated by. Those questions tend to be the useful ones.

I left teaching and moved into UX design.

People describe it as a leap. It felt more like pointing the same instinct at a different object. In a classroom I watched where someone got stuck, changed the explanation, and tried again. A lot of design is that: find the moment of confusion and treat it as your problem, not the user's.

What didn't come with me was the portfolio, the tools, or the confidence. I took a pay cut. I asked basic questions in rooms where everyone else already had the vocabulary. Around month four I nearly convinced myself I'd made a foolish choice.

Teaching still shows up in the work. I listen longer. I don't assume the person using the product failed. I can explain a decision to someone who wasn't in the room when we made it.

If you're looking at a change that seems unrelated on paper, look at the skill under the title. Mine was helping someone through the hard part. That was never only a teaching skill.

Saying no is the least pleasant skill that improved my work.

I used to agree and then resent the week. Yes to the meeting, yes to the extra project, yes to the quick look that wasn't quick. None of them were disasters alone. Stacked up, they pushed out the work I'd already said yes to.

It still feels rude for a few seconds. Then the week happens and I remember why I did it. A no is how I keep a real commitment to someone else. It also means admitting I can't do all of it well, which I knew and kept trying to outrun.

I keep the wording short: I can't take this on and do it properly. Sometimes there's a smaller version I can offer. Sometimes there isn't.

I'm not consistent. I am less buried than I used to be, and more of what I accepted actually gets finished.

Congratulations to Priya on her new role as CTO.

I got to work with her before the title matched the job she was already doing. She makes hard calls without making them about herself. She'll tell you why. She stays close to the details and still leaves the work with the people who own it.

Teams get better around her. I hope this role gives her more room to do that.

Very well earned, Priya. Excited to see what you build next.

I just finished my first year as a freelance designer. A few things I didn't understand in month one:

Pricing is its own skill. I undercharged the projects I was excited about, then felt strange about the work, which didn't help the client or me.

The brief is half the job. When I skipped the questions up front, I paid for it in revisions. Most of the time the client wasn't being difficult. They were reacting to a gap I left open.

Quiet months make you want to take everything. Some of those yeses cost me a better project that showed up two weeks later.

And the admin is the job too. Contracts, invoices, chasing a signature. The design is the part that looks like the work. The rest is why it becomes a business.

I like it. It isn't the carefree version people post about. It's a small business with one employee, and the employee is me. This year I'm raising my rates and getting faster at the questions I should have asked the first time.
